documents.abstract: This systematic review examines interventions designed to regulate cognitive offloading to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and their effects on subsequent independent performance in educational and employee development contexts. The review aims to identify how interventions structure the distribution of cognitive work between individuals and GenAI, evaluate their effects on learning and task performance after AI assistance has been withdrawn, and examine the conditions under which these effects may differ. Eligible evidence will include comparative experimental and quasi-experimental studies assessing independent knowledge, skills or task performance following GenAI-supported activities. Electronic searches were conducted in six bibliographic databases and preprint repositories, followed by deduplication and pilot screening. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data. The review will use structured descriptive synthesis, supplemented by meta-analysis where the evidence permits. Risk of bias will be assessed using JBI tools, and certainty of evidence for key outcomes will be evaluated using GRADE. The expected contribution is an evidence-based understanding of which approaches to regulating cognitive offloading have been evaluated, what effects they produce on independent performance, and how confidently these effects can be interpreted. Findings may inform the design of GenAI-supported education and employee development activities.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges for AI-generated content, yet a single judge is unreliable and even a panel of judges leaves a hard residue: when judges disagree, majority voting simply discards the conflict instead of resolving it. We present JuryFlow, a disagreement-guided, human-in-the-loop multi-agent evaluation framework that treats inter-judge disagreement not as noise to be averaged away, but as a precise, claim-level signal indicating where an evaluation is uncertain. JuryFlow decomposes each candidate response into atomic claims, has a panel of heterogeneous judges assign per-claim verdicts, and builds a disagreement graph whose nodes are scored by verdict entropy and whose edges encode structural similarity between claims. A human acts as a structural guide, i.e., selecting which disagreement to resolve through a single, minimal intervention rather than re-labeling the response, after which the focal claim is re-evaluated, the correction propagates along graph edges and to historically similar cases, and is crystallized into reusable rubric entries that all judges inherit, making the evaluator progressively self-refining. To enable large-scale, reproducible benchmarking without human studies, we evaluate JuryFlow in an automatic configuration in which the focal selection is made by entropy ranking. On MT-Bench and LLMBar, JuryFlow improves agreement with gold labels over single-judge and majority-vote panel baselines, and ablations isolate the contributions of disagreement-targeted re-evaluation, propagation, and rubric induction. We contribute (1) a human-in-the-loop paradigm that recasts the human from labeler to structural guide, (2) the JuryFlow framework operationalizing it through a disagreement graph, focal re-evaluation, and closed-loop rubric induction, and (3) an evaluation protocol with ablations that isolate where the gains originate.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: There is growing interest in understanding how people interact with large language models (LLMs) and whether such models elicit dependency or even addictive behaviour. Validated tools to assess the extent to which individuals may become dependent on LLMs are scarce and primarily build on classic behavioural addiction symptoms, adapted to the context of LLM use. We view this as a conceptual limitation, as the LLM-human relationship is more nuanced and warrants a fresh and distinct perspective. To address this gap, we developed and validated a new 12-item questionnaire to measure LLM dependency, referred to as LLM-D12. The scale was based on the authors’ prior theoretical work, with items developed accordingly and responses collected from 526 participants in the UK. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, performed on separate halves of the total sample using a split-sample approach, supported a two-factor structure: Instrumental Dependency (six items) and Relationship Dependency (six items). Instrumental Dependency reflects the extent to which individuals rely on LLMs to support or collaborate in decision-making and cognitive tasks. Relationship Dependency captures the tendency to perceive LLMs as socially meaningful, sentient, or companion-like entities. The two-factor structure demonstrated excellent internal consistency and clear discriminant validity. External validation confirmed both the conceptual foundation and the distinction between the two subscales. The psychometric properties and structure of our LLM-D12 scale were interpreted in light of the emerging view that dependency on LLMs does not necessarily indicate dysfunction but may still reflect reliance levels that could become problematic in certain contexts.

Evaluating whether an AI agent behaves like a good teammate is becoming a bottleneck as multi-agent language-model systems proliferate, because human ratings do not scale to the transcripts these systems generate. We ask whether a language model can stand in for a human rater of teammate quality, offering a controlled proof-of-concept validation rather than a large-scale study. Drawing on the autonomous-agent teammate-likeness construct from the human-autonomy-teaming literature, we define a six-dimension behavioral coding scheme covering altruistic, benevolent, interdependent, emotive, communicative, and synchronized conduct, adapted for a language-model judge. We validate it by rewriting the partner’s lines in team-task transcripts as cooperative, neutral, or defective while holding the rest fixed, and having five judges from five model families rate every version. Every judge orders the manipulated behavior as intended and every pair agrees on relative ordering, though absolute calibration differs by up to about a scale point. On registers matched for length and politeness the judges separate cooperative from degraded conduct but resolve subtle defection only weakly; a blinded single-rater human pilot reproduces both the orderings and that limit. The scheme is therefore valid for relative comparisons but not for absolute thresholds applied across judges. We give design implications for LLM-judge teaming evaluation, and release the scheme, stimuli, prompts, and ratings.

Digital Twin (DT) systems are increasingly applied to domestic energy management, distributing decision-making across sensors, algorithms, and users. Designing for shared agency requires making this distribution explicit. This paper characterises engagement in domestic DTs through two lenses: Digital Twin Engagement Style (Visibility × Proactivity) and User Engagement Style (Intentionality × Activeness). These dimensions make system initiative, information visibility, user intentions, and behavioral activity designable. The framework helps designers identify alignments and tensions between user and system engagement, and trace how agency shifts across interaction configurations. Future work will apply the framework to design cases to develop concrete guidelines and assess its practical usefulness.

Conversational AI often places navigation cost on users by requiring them to continuously steer conversations, articulate preferences, and monitor AI responses. Reducing this cost may require giving AI systems more conversational initiative, raising questions about how this shift affects users’ agency and responsibility. We explore a 2-on-1 AI deliberation design, where users overhear two agents’ discussion and intervene when needed. Informed by a formative study, our system pairs a Personalized AI representing the user’s preferences with an Expert AI providing alternative perspectives. In a within-subjects mixed-methods study on travel planning, 2-on-1 deliberation reduced navigation cost and perceived agency, while we observed no statistically detectable difference in decision responsibility across conditions. Qualitative findings suggest that users shifted from steering the conversation to overhearing, evaluating, and selectively intervening in agent-to-agent deliberation. We discuss overhearing as an evaluative mode of participation in AI deliberation systems.

In AI-assisted decision-making, achieving warranted trust is essential: users should follow accurate advice while rejecting wrong suggestions. But as LLM-based AI agents reshape decision support, such agents often display miscalibrated confidence – ranging from confidently incorrect hallucinations to overly non-committal hedging. To understand how this behavior and unannounced system changes impact user trust, we conducted a two-phase online study (N=90) evaluating advice-seeking and reliance after confidence calibration is silently updated. We found that users’ willingness to seek AI advice is driven overwhelmingly by their pre-existing (positive) attitudes toward AI, not by the system’s prior performance. However, once they actively consult the AI, their reliance is significantly higher if they previously encountered a confidently incorrect or a non-committal system rather than a calibrated baseline. This effect dampens over time, with qualitative insights showing how unannounced background changes can erode perceived quality. These findings demonstrate that safe AI integration requires addressing individual user biases and transparently communicating updates.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: University students occasionally struggle to ask questions in class. While AI can support learning, little is known about how it can support in-class question asking. We developed an AI system that generates questions in real time from lecture content and a mobile interface that allows students to view, vote on, and submit their own questions alongside AI-generated ones. We deployed this system in four computer-science lectures, and found that AI-generated questions helped students consider lecture content from different perspectives. For some, this prompted deeper reflection on what to ask. However, others reported reduced motivation to form their own questions, suggesting risks of overreliance. Although students found the AI helpful, they more frequently voted for questions asked by their peers, revealing a gap between AI-generated questions and students’ in-the-moment learning needs. We provide design recommendations for systems that promote interactive collaboration with AI and scaffold question asking without undermining student agency.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: While HCI has expanded from Personal to Family Informatics, researchers still lack a critical analytical vocabulary to diagnose what truly constitutes a collective care context. We introduce Sangyadhi, an analytical sociotechnical framework that synthesizes Situated Action, Distributed Cognition, the Capabilities Approach, and Actor-Network Theory to investigate multi-actor care ecologies. The framework articulates four interdependent analytical lenses: contextual grounding, distributed responsibility, trust-mediated sharing, and collaborative actionability. To demonstrate its diagnostic utility, we apply Sangyadhi to critically audit a decade of HCI digital health literature across self-tracking, family informatics, and clinical AI---surfacing structural omissions in how shifting authority, dynamic trust, and AI escalation are conceptualized. Ultimately, the goal of Sangyadhi is to equip researchers with an analytical blueprint for diagnosing observed care contexts, structuring field inquiries, and evaluating future technologies.

Objective: To analyze the effects of Integrative Community Therapy (ICT) on self-perceived happiness and emotional well-being among slaughterhouse workers in a Brazilian municipality located on an international border. Methods: This exploratory quasi-experimental study was grounded in the ICT framework and conducted in Itaipulândia, Paraná, from April to December 2019. The McDowell and Newell Faces Scale was used to assess self-perceived happiness before and after ICT circles, alongside a sociodemographic questionnaire and an analysis of universal themes and coping strategies that emerged during the circles. Results: Twelve circles were held with 151 workers. Self-perceived happiness and emotional state improved significantly after the circles. The main universal themes were physical health problems, bereavement, family conflict, and stress, revealing the connection between emotional suffering and the work context. The most common coping strategies were seeking spiritual or religious support, strengthening family relationships, and personal empowerment. Workers aged 18–24 years had 4.28 times greater odds of emotional improvement after participating in the circles than workers older than 24 years. Conclusion: ICT showed promise as a relationship-centered care strategy in occupational health, supporting improved self-perceived happiness and emotional well-being and strengthening support networks among slaughterhouse workers. Collective and integrative care strategies may be particularly valuable in work settings marked by physical and psychosocial vulnerability.

Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Applied studies of employee performance in Indonesian technical firms usually ask which factor dominates. This study asks instead whether technical competence, occupational health and safety (OHS), and the work environment behave as rival levers or as a bundle of resources. A census survey of all 41 employees of PT Multi Jaya Teknik, an electrical and mechanical contractor in Batu Bara Regency, North Sumatra, measured each construct with a five-item Likert scale (α = .807-.903), and performance was regressed on the three predictors by ordinary least squares. The predictors jointly explained a large share of variance, R² = .602 (adjusted R² = .570), F(3, 37) = 18.65, p < .001. Technical competence (B = 0.372, 95% CI [0.035, 0.709], f² = 0.135), OHS (B = 0.290, 95% CI [0.048, 0.532], f² = 0.159), and work environment (B = 0.261, 95% CI [0.018, 0.504], f² = 0.127) each retained a unique positive association, with closely matched standardized weights (β = .267-.335) and overlapping intervals. Because the smallest individual effect the design could detect was f² = 0.202, each estimate is individually fragile, whereas the joint effect is clear. The pattern is interpreted as safe competence: in hazardous field work, capability, safety provision, and workable conditions act as non-redundant resources, so no single lever should be expected to dominate. The study also shows that perceived OHS provision predicts self-rated performance, not accident prevention, and it offers a complete reporting template for small single-firm samples.

What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Hospitals and health systems are complex adaptive systems. Safe care, continuity of services and the ability to adapt under pressure all depend on people noticing what is happening, making sense of it and anticipating what comes next. Situational awareness (SA), a concept that grew out of military aviation and human factors engineering, is now built into clinical non-technical skills frameworks, organisational resilience models and crisis management practice.

This article asks how a scientific, evidence-generating approach can speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare. We use LifeLink Monitoring as an applied case and combine a structured literature review, market and regulatory analysis, competitive benchmarking, stakeholder surveys and expert interviews, scenario modelling, and pilot design. The analysis reveals a persistent shortage of context-specific evidence on clinical utility, workflow integration, human factors, economics, and governance. To address it, we propose an Evidence-to-Adoption Framework in which staged pilots turn technological hypotheses into evidence that clinicians, managers, regulators, payers, and investors can act on. We treat acceleration as a proposed mechanism that requires prospective testing, not as a demonstrated outcome, and we specify how it can be measured.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Unsignalized roundabouts remain challenging for connected and autonomous vehicles because of dynamic merges, spatial conflicts, and communication constraints. We present a decentralized coordination architecture based on Group Mutual Exclusion (GME), in which each conflict point is treated as a local critical section and compatible virtual platoons may be admitted concurrently. A lead vehicle aggregates requests from its physical queue and relays admission decisions to following vehicles. To make this safety-critical process intelligible to occupants, we introduce a query-driven small language model (SLM) interface that reads structured controller traces and produces explanations only when requested. The SLM is strictly read-only and cannot alter GME decisions. We illustrate how traces containing conflict, priority, and waiting-time information can support contextual explanations of yielding, deceleration, and merging. The work provides an architecture and feasibility demonstration. Quantitative traffic, language-model, and human-factors evaluations are left to future work.

Reliance on artificial agents involves at least two decisions: whether to use the system and whether to verify its output. We examined how trust and self-reported verification fatigue were associated with these dimensions in survey responses from 390 adults across six English-speaking countries. Trust was strongly associated with AI use frequency (β =.50), whereas verification fatigue was not (β =.05). Fatigue was instead associated with verification skipping (β =.36) and selective verification (β =.31) but not reliably with active verification, and these two coefficients did not differ (Δβ =.05, p =.382). Trust was associated only with skipping among the three effort-graded verification behaviors, and its coefficient was larger for skipping than for selective verification (Δβ =.12, p =.040). No interaction survived correction. This pattern is consistent with trust relating to perceived verification necessity and self-reported verification fatigue to perceived verification burden, two routes converging on verification skipping; however, the cross-sectional self-report design cannot establish these mechanisms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could make personalized tutoring available at scale, but it remains unclear how they can best support the instructional processes that make one-on-one instruction effective. We compared two ways of using LLMs after students make errors: providing personalized explanations of those errors, or engaging students in additional cycles of scaffolded practice and feedback, with a Socratic tutor guiding students toward the correct answer. In a preregistered online experiment, 400 adults practiced setting up constraint equations and, after each attempt, received the correct answer, a generic explanation, a personalized LLM explanation of their error, or Socratic tutoring. Socratic tutoring helped: participants resolved 64% of their errors through the dialogue and scored 0.24 SD higher on practice-aligned posttest questions than those who received generic or personalized explanations. Socratic participants also found the session more interesting, less frustrating, and less costly, even though it took nearly twice as long. In contrast, we found no evidence of a benefit of personalized explanations over generic ones, and neither type of explanation reliably outperformed simply seeing the correct answer. These findings suggest that LLM tutors may add the most value not by explaining errors more precisely but by helping students correct those errors themselves through scaffolded practice. This pattern fits a mastery-experience account of tutoring, in which an effective tutor notices when a student is struggling, steps in with guidance, and works with the student until the struggle resolves into success. AI tutors may be most effective when designed around this principle.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.

documents.abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.

A basic AI label reveals that AI was involved but says little about how the resulting advice was produced or reviewed. This study tests a first-stage moderated mediation model in which transparency messages relate to self-reported willingness to follow AI-mediated financial advice through perceived trustworthiness, conditional on AI role. In a six-condition between-subjects experiment (N = 227), participants received the same portfolio recommendation across three transparency conditions (no disclosure, basic AI disclosure, and detailed explanation) and two AI-role framings (primary source and support tool). The no-disclosure conditions formed a common participant-facing baseline in which AI role was not communicated. Within the support-tool reference condition, basic disclosure did not increase perceived trustworthiness relative to no disclosure, whereas the detailed message increased trustworthiness relative to both no disclosure and basic disclosure. Perceived trustworthiness was strongly associated with willingness to follow the recommendation (b = 1.018, p <.001). The detailed-message × AI-role interaction was significant (b = −.291, 95% CI [ −.450, −.132]), and the detailed-versus-no-disclosure indirect effect through trustworthiness excluded zero in the support-tool condition (indirect effect =.504, 95% bootstrap CI [.032,.976]) but not in the primary-source condition. Because the detailed messages also differed in whether human review was present, the interaction captures differences between advisory-message configurations rather than a pure effect of explanation depth or AI role. The findings advance a content-sensitive account of AI transparency: labels alone were insufficient, while what transparency communicated about advice production, decision authority, and human review was consequential for trustworthiness judgments and willingness to follow AI-mediated advice.

Children increasingly use AI agents that can act on their own. Yet, many agentic systems are designed around a capable user, one who can judge a response, absorb an error, and speak up for their own needs, and who thereby serves as the final check on an overstepping system. A child user is not a small adult [29], and children’s ability to interpret and rely on an agent is still developing. Systems that rely on the child’s judgment as their source of human oversight therefore pose real dangers in exactly the moments that matter most [25, 28]. We propose that the agent can supply this check, and refer the child to a trusted adult. This action complements existing methods such as content-based refusal, confidence-based abstention, fixed age-gating, and emotional-safety filtering. Beyond asking whether a request is permissible or an answer confident, the agent also asks whether the situation is one it should handle alone. Taking the developing child into consideration, we identify the circumstances in which an agent should not act alone and specify the response each calls for. These situations form the basis of a research agenda that we plan to develop into benchmarks and design resources for child-facing agents.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the perceived credibility of AI- versus human-written news. A 3×2×2 online experiment (N = 480) finds that human-written and human–AI collaborative news are rated more credible than AI-generated news, mediated by perceived accountability; media type and news type did not moderate the effects. The study informs trust in human–machine journalism and responsible AI use.
topics: News Media Framing and Political Communication

documents.abstract: As social agents, robots, conversational AI systems, and virtual characters become embedded in everyday environments, HAI is shifting from isolated one-human/one-agent interaction toward socially embedded multi-person and multi-agent settings. This workshop explores how trust, blame, and responsibility emerge, become distributed, and are negotiated among users, agents, developers, institutions, bystanders, and broader social contexts. We focus on agents as social participants in complex environments, including group dynamics, psychological safety, agent refusal, moral consideration, and legal or governance questions. The workshop aims to develop a preliminary issue map, research agenda, and interdisciplinary network for socially sustainable human-agent societies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As teleoperated systems increasingly incorporate autonomous agents capable of independent decision-making, the human operator transitions from a direct controller to a delegated supervisor. This shift introduces a fundamental challenge: how operators calibrate their trust toward agents whose decisions they cannot interpret. Miscalibrated trust, whether overtrust leading to unsafe delegation or undertrust causing inefficient over-intervention, represents one of the most consequential human factors risks in agentic teleoperation. This paper argues that Explainable AI (XAI) mechanisms constitute a promising but underexplored lever for dynamic trust calibration in teleoperated human-agent systems. A three-layer conceptual framework is proposed that maps operator profiles to adaptive XAI modality selection and closes the loop through a trust feedback mechanism that dynamically adjusts the agent’s level of autonomy. Three application scenarios, namely robotic surgical assistance, hazardous environment inspection, and remote industrial maintenance, are examined to illustrate how the framework operates under realistic teleoperation constraints. The paper identifies key research challenges and outlines a forward-looking agenda for empirically grounding the proposed framework.

Предложена модель трёх контуров делегирования — инструментального, тьюторского и партнёрского — а также четыре критерия выбора контура и принципы проектирования заданий и оценивания, снижающие риск утраты формируемого навыка. Приведён рабочий чек-лист преподавателя.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now perform many academic tasks that students were once required to master, raising the question of whether learners still value learning for themselves and feel capable of learning without relying on AI. Available scales mainly focus on AI as the outcome of learning rather than the context of it. This study developed and validated brief scales measuring Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI, the value of personally learning when associated tasks can be performed by AI) and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI, the appraisal of ability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI) and examined their associations with AI use and academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence, GPA). Data were collected from 882 undergraduate students in the U.S. with approximately equal traditional-age and adult learners. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis supported a correlated two-factor structure. Both scales showed acceptable reliability (ω = .81 and .72), discriminant validity from classical task value and self-efficacy, and measurement invariance across student age type. When classical task value, classical self-efficacy, and AI use were controlled, LV-AI and LSE-AI incrementally predicted effort and persistence, but not GPA. Moreover, although AI use showed a significant negative association with academic effort, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that this association no longer held when learners' LV-AI and LSE-AI were accounted for, with the indirect path carrying over half of the initial association. This highlights the important role these AI-embedded constructs play in preventing the disengagement tendencies.

In this paper the author argues that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has not created a new form of academic misconduct. Rather, it has taken the least-policed form of misconduct we had, that of cutting corners, and stripped it of the three properties that made it survivable. This 'sloppiness' was coupled to effort, bounded to one paper, and attributable to someone who lacked diligence. Fluent prose was once an 'honest signal', because it was costly to fake, and the apparatus of peer review built upon that cost. GenAI has broken that signal. Other things have broken too, including the evidence chain. 'Citation laundering' is where a fabricated claim, cited once by an author linking it to a real source, acquires a provenance despite it being unreachable by any reference check. The author highlights research in health professions education in which various authors have admitted to citing work they have not read, and argues that current GenAI use declarations are largely uncalibrated instruments. The closest look health professions education scholars seem to have taken at their own reference lists appears to predate these tools, and because syntheses inform guidelines and guidelines inform curricula, a fabricated claim can travel from a 'prompt' to what a clinician teaches at the bedside. Because journals' workflows have not traditionally involved verification, blame for abuses all too often falls on reviewers, who are ill equipped to carry it. Ultimately, the use of GenAI means that much of our cognitive effort needs to be relocated from the act of writing into a deliberate act of adjudication. The author describes how this paper was itself produced using GenAI to bring back effortful, bounded and attributable practice leading to a worked example of disclosure that describes practice rather than certifying intention.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

Initial public offerings in China pass through a dense chain of gatekeepers: sponsors, auditors, exchange reviewers, the securities regulator, and a retail-dominated investor base. Artificial intelligence now enters every link in that chain at once. It writes disclosures, verifies them, screens them for regulators, informs the investors who price them, and increasingly forms the core of the issuers that seek listing. This paper develops a theory of how AI disrupts an IPO market that operates as a state-orchestrated certification system. Drawing on signaling theory, the economics of certification, institutional theory, and the view of AI as an entrepreneurial actor, we argue that AI lowers the cost of producing information while leaving the cost of producing credible information intact. Seven propositions trace where the residual cost of credibility moves: toward an inverted U-shaped link between AI-generated disclosure and informativeness, a shift in intermediary rents from reputation to verification, an advantage for algorithmically legible issuers, an earlier inflection point in the effect of positive sentiment on IPO performance, attribution-dependent penalties for AI issuers, scope-contingent gains for intermediaries, and state pacing as a boundary condition. The theory explains why AI can raise market throughput and lower signal informativeness at the same time.

AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Context: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) assistants are now part of everyday software engineering work, where developers and students must decide how far to rely on fluent outputs of opaque provenance. Evaluation usually treats reliability as a binary label (true/false, hallucinated/not), which ignores the communicative mode, evidentiary standard, and stakes under which people calibrate trust. Objective: We model statement reliability as a context-conditioned distribution of community endorsement and test whether and to what extent access to verification resources produces measurable, item-dependent signatures in that distribution. Method: The framework represents a statement’s status as a contextual agreement state : the distribution of commitments that a declared community assigns under an explicitly declared context (mode, evidentiary standard, scope, stakes, domain). A bet-based operational semantics makes correspondence truth a limiting case of the framework. In a between-subjects classroom study (about 120 students, session-level random allocation), participants rated six statements without or with external help (web search, GenAI assistants, and other resources). Results: For three of the four statements classified a priori as stable-referent, help raised belief (Cliff’s 𝛿 = 0 . 3 8 –0.43), and dispersion tended to fall (standard-deviation ratios 0.82–0.87; significant for one statement). For both a priori contested statements, belief location barely changed ( 𝛿 = − 0 . 1 1 and 0.07), while responses polarised (ratios 1.35 and 1.48; both significant). The direction of dispersion change matched the a priori family for five of six statements, as did the direction of the mean shift; the exception for dispersion, a historical statement, behaved like a contested one and was reclassified post hoc. Conclusion: Dispersion under verification is a measurable, decision-relevant complement to truth labels and confidence scores. The evidence is preliminary: six items, one cohort, and a composite help condition that does not isolate the contribution of GenAI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The diffusion of Industry 4.0 technologies, including artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and robotics, is transforming manufacturing by increasing efficiency, customization, and flexibility. At the same time, adoption has exposed a substantial skills gap, particularly in advanced technical capabilities and higher-order problem-solving. This study examines the sources of this gap by focusing on misalignment between educational and industry needs, organizational resistance to upskilling, and the rising demand for cross-disciplinary expertise. The study draws on 43 semi-structured interviews with industry and academic experts across 27 countries, analyzed with the Gioia methodology. The findings identify recurring barriers, including outdated training provision, underinvestment in reskilling, and weak collaboration between academia and industry. The results also point to the need to institutionalize continuous learning and to strengthen industry-led workforce transformation through coordinated partnerships and policy incentives. Building on these findings, the paper proposes the Smart Manufacturing Skills Framework (SMSF). The framework links three layers of competence to a continuous learning loop and represents the conditions under which competence is formed, absorbed, and renewed. The mechanisms connecting these conditions are stated as four propositions for future research. The paper concludes with practical recommendations centered on targeted training pathways, government support mechanisms, and lifelong learning strategies to improve workforce readiness for smart manufacturing.

The digitalization of internal control is widely presented as a lever of performance, yet the mechanisms behind this contribution remain unclear. This article argues that the dominant readings of the phenomenon, whether technical, compliance-based, or resource-based, share a common assumption: they treat digitalization as a state rather than as an ability, which prevents them from explaining why comparable tools produce different outcomes and why well-performing control systems become obsolete. Drawing on an integrative literature review and a theory adaptation approach, the article reinterprets internal control digitalization through dynamic capabilities theory. It distinguishes technological resources, operational capabilities, and dynamic capabilities, and defines internal control digitalization as a capability combining continuous risk sensing, deliberate response, and ongoing reconfiguration of the control system. This reinterpretation uncovers a tension between reconfiguration and the stability on which control reliability rests, and introduces the concept of reconfiguration governance, which is distinguished from IT change management and structured around five dimensions. Six propositions follow. The capability affects organizational performance mainly through two parallel and partial mediators, risk management effectiveness and internal control reliability, provided that data are of adequate quality and that automated controls remain under human oversight. Reconfiguration governance determines whether the capability strengthens or weakens control reliability, environmental dynamism moderates the relationship in an inverted U-shaped manner, and institutional pressures weaken it only when they lead to symbolic adoption. The article confronts these propositions with competing arguments, situates them in the Moroccan textile sector, and proposes an operationalization with a view to their empirical validation.

Algorithmic and AI systems employed in public administration often manifest technocratic and efficiency premises which may conflict with the democratic and socio-technical fundaments of algorithmic practices in government. Partially, these premises are infused into these public algorithmic systems during the design process. This paper conducts a case study in a consortium of Dutch public organisations that reshapes design practices of algorithmic systems to uncover institutional logics underlying these practices. Our observations and interviews at the consortium of 13 public organisations revealed four design practices that deviate from sociotechnical design practices: (1) distance from politics, (2) underrate the input from non-technical experts, (3) operate on a procurement-oriented dynamic, and (4) follow a chronological phasing combined with agile or scrum practices. Through abductive reasoning, we derived the technocratic and businesslike logics that shaped these design practices. These institutional logics clash with the socio-technical, political, and material nature of public algorithmic systems. To arrive at more responsible, accountable and ethical use of these systems in government, public organisations need to modify their design practices. Our findings provide initial insights into the institutional logics required to change design practices, while also underscoring the complexity of altering routines and practices that are deeply rooted in organisational structures and cultures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the relationship between digital platform acceptance and entrepreneurial intentions among early-career digital entrepreneurship learners by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behaviour. Data were collected from participants across Indonesia and China, recruited through entrepreneurship training programmes and digital business communities, who had exposure to various digital entrepreneurship platforms. PLS-SEM analysis reveals that Perceived Behavioural Control emerges as the strongest predictor of Entrepreneurship Intention, closely followed by Digital Entrepreneurship Resilience. Digital Entrepreneurship Resilience partially mediates the relationships between both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness with Entrepreneurship Intention. The structural model explains 62.5% of the variance in entrepreneurship intention. However, the hypothesised moderating effect of Perceived Behavioural Control on the resilience-intention relationship does not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest that entrepreneurial intention development requires more than technology exposure alone, emphasising the critical roles of perceived control and adaptive capacity in digital contexts. Practical implications indicate that digital entrepreneurship training programmes should deliberately cultivate both technological resilience and behavioural control through platform-based experiential learning rather than focusing exclusively on technical skills.

Abstract Background Giving meaningful feedback on assignments in large introductory-level mathematics courses is a challenge. The emergence of “out of the box” Large Language Models (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) has created a potential solution to this challenge, where the AI tool can be trained to give constructive feedback on student work. However, it is unclear whether these tools are sufficiently accurate, efficient, and trustworthy. The current study investigates the use of a bespoke AI tool to assist in giving feedback to students in two introductory mathematics courses that enroll over 400 students each and are characterized by high attrition. Results We evaluated the similarities in grades assigned by the AI tool and human graders, as well as student and grader perceptions of the feedback given by both the AI tool and human graders. We found that the tool was fairly accurate, but that perceptions of the utility of its feedback varied by condition. When evaluated as a stand-alone grading agent, the AI tool was significantly undervalued relative to human graders—both student peers and the professor. Conclusion Three themes that characterize our findings: student trust is key, the professor is irreplaceable, and graders and AI tools must be carefully trained to ensure accuracy, transparency, and trust. We conclude with a call to exercise caution in using these tools in grading assistance, particularly with respect to maintaining student trust and transparency in grading.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: As automated driving systems (ADS) become increasingly integrated into real-world transportation, understanding how human drivers perceive and respond to system failures under adversarial conditions is critical for driving safety. Prior research has shown that human drivers overestimate ADS capabilities and lack awareness of ADS vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We conduct a laboratory study (N=32) using a driving simulator, investigating the effectiveness of explanations on enhancing human drivers' situation awareness (SA) of physical adversarial evasion attacks and their takeover performance in SAE Level 3 automated driving. We varied system reliability and attack object within subjects and explanation between subjects. Quantitative results indicated that explanations enhanced drivers' SA, without deteriorating their takeover performance. The reliability manipulation yielded non-significant results in general, probably because of explanatory content presented for the ADS detected-and-handled attacks. Nevertheless, we obtained the impact of attack object on drivers' takeover control regardless of the explanation manipulation. Qualitative results revealed that drivers often noticed abnormalities without recognizing them as attacks, while perceiving explanations as useful aids for understanding scenarios. We discuss implications of our findings and directions of future work.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly make decisions that unfold over time: autonomous vehicles navigating traffic, robots executing manipulation sequences, game-playing agents taking moves toward their goals, and planning systems constructing multistep action sequences. Explaining such sequential behavior is fundamentally harder than explaining a single classification or regression output, yet this challenge has only recently received sustained research attention across the reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, and game-AI communities. This chapter provides an introduction to Explainable AI for Sequential Decision-Making (X-SDM). A unified taxonomy is developed that answers four core questions: what must be explained, who needs the explanation, how are explanations generated algorithmically, and how should they be evaluated. The taxonomy spans formal models including Markov Decision Processes and symbolic planning and covers the major families of explanation methods that have emerged across communities: contrastive and counterfactual explanations, feature importance and attribution methods, plan and goal explanations, model-reconciliation explanations, and intrinsically interpretable policies. These categories are illustrated with representative techniques, and a principled framework for user requirements grounded in situation-awareness theory is sketched. The chapter closes with ten open research questions that chart a roadmap for the field. The chapter integrates perspectives from reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, game AI, and cognitive science, offering students and researchers a structured entry point into this growing area.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini have become part of daily academic life, but little is known about how pre-service teachers use them to deal with academic problems or how teachers perceive their influence on students’ problem-solving. This qualitative, phenomenologically oriented study investigated (a) how final-semester B.Ed. students apply generative AI tools to their academic problems, and (b) how university teachers perceive the influence of AI tools on students’ problem-solving skills and what guidance they offer for productive AI use. Semi-structured interviews was conducted with twenty-three students and thirteen teachers from five public universities in Lahore, Pakistan, and the data was analyzed using thematic analysis. Two student themes were developed: patterns and purposes of AI use in academic work, and deciding between AI and independent effort. Two teacher themes were developed: teachers’ observations of AI use and its perceived influence on problem-solving, and teachers’ guidance, difficulties, and advice for productive AI use. Students reported regular use of AI for assignments, presentations, research, and lesson planning; thirteen tried problems independently first, while nine turned to AI first. All thirteen teachers observed regular and growing use of AI and agreed that it helps students understand concepts and explore approaches, but all thirteen also feared that heavy dependence could weaken critical thinking and independence. Teachers advised students to attempt tasks first, verify AI output, and write final work in their own words. Because the findings rest on participants’ reported views, they describe perceptions and not measured effects on problem-solving ability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Expressing dynamic events in Mixed Reality (MR) requires users to communicate continuous spatiotemporal information, including entity trajectories, interactions, and temporal dynamics. This task is fundamentally constrained by the linearization bottleneck: human mental models preserve rich relational structures holistically, yet conventional output channels, such as speech, force them to be serialized into sequential streams. Multimodal interaction offers a promising solution by distributing information across complementary channels, but it remains unclear how different multimodal strategies perform as spatiotemporal complexity increases. This paper addresses these two knowledge gaps: the lack of a systematic analysis of decomposing dynamic events and the absence of empirical evidence comparing multimodal expression strategies under controlled-complexity conditions. We propose a structured analysis that decomposes dynamic events into fundamental information blocks and establishes a complexity taxonomy. Building on this analysis, we design sequential and parallel multimodal expression strategies and evaluate them alongside sequential (unimodal) speech as complete interaction strategies in a controlled user study using abstract geometric micro-worlds. Under error-free speech–gaze fusion provided through a Wizard-of-Oz setup, parallel multimodal input maintains a substantial completion-time advantage across the tested event levels. However, its subjective benefits decrease as coordination demands rise. When events include asynchronous timing or causal interactions, parallel input is no longer rated significantly higher than sequential multimodal input, though this does not imply equivalence. These findings suggest a boundary condition for the subjective benefits of the parallel strategy, providing design implications for adaptive multimodal MR systems.

Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are fundamentally constructed upon the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm. This paradigm can be characterized as an ill-posed optimization problem within a high-dimensional parameter space. When confronted with real-world scenarios characterized by noise and conflicting constraints, the logic of global error minimization inherently induces a strong smoothing effect. Consequently, this yields statistical compromise solutions that flatten local features, making it arduous to overcome the inherent bottleneck of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing AI models generate outputs purely based on statistical probabilities. They lack the capacity to autonomously discern truth from falsehood or establish causal logic, thereby lacking genuine cognitive intelligence. To address the ontological limitations of the OD paradigm, this paper proposes a novel paradigm termed \textit{Structure-Enabled Intelligence}. This approach abandons the conventional path of relying solely on computing power scaling and data fitting to achieve emergent intelligence. Instead, it embeds mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as underlying priors into the algorithmic architecture, constraining the model's solving process with structured scientific rules. Through this paradigm shift from ``data-driven objective fitting'' to ``mechanism-structure dominance,'' the proposed approach fundamentally mitigates the issue of statistical compromise, enhances the model's extrapolation and generalization capabilities, and simultaneously reshapes human-AI synergy by upholding human subjectivity in scientific cognition.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of university students’ everyday learning, yet research on its consequences has focused mainly on immediate learning outcomes. This study examined whether the way students use generative AI in their studies is connected with how they appraise their professional futures. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading, appraisal theories of stress and emotion, and career construction theory, I tested whether AI dependence—letting AI do the cognitive work of learning tasks and accepting its output with little verification—rather than frequency of use was associated with anxiety about post-graduation destinations, whether perceived AI threat accounted for part of this association, and whether career adaptability buffered the threat–anxiety link. In a cross-sectional survey of 965 Chinese university students, AI dependence was positively associated with post-graduation anxiety when frequency was controlled (β = .36), whereas frequency was not (β = .00). Perceived AI threat accounted for an indirect association amounting to 41% of the total. Career adaptability was associated with lower anxiety, but, contrary to the buffering hypothesis, the threat–anxiety association was stronger among more adaptable students, and adaptability was unrelated to anxiety when perceived threat was high. In exploratory analyses, critical use of AI output was associated with higher adaptability but not with threat or anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings are associations compatible with the proposed pathway rather than evidence of causation. Implications for AI-integrated teaching and assessment, AI literacy, and career guidance in higher education are discussed.

Agentic AI systems increasingly execute actions for users, including transfers, deployments, account changes, and data release. Human approval gates are meant to prevent these actions from running until a reviewer has inspected the proposed action and issued a decision. Because approval can arrive after a delay, frameworks often persist workflow state and resume later. The resume path therefore becomes a security boundary: it must distinguish evidence that a human approved from approval-shaped values stored in mutable state. We define Approval-Provenance Failure as a condition in which a workflow resume path treats mutable approval-relevant state as evidence that a trusted human approval path produced a decision. Our adversary can write approval-relevant workflow state, but cannot use the approval path, change the model, modify tool code, invoke the tool directly, write the business database, mint a valid approval artifact, or access the approval issuer key. We evaluate 18 agent frameworks with human approval, interruption, or pause-resume behavior. Thirteen are exposed, three are resistant, and two are non-applicable. In exposed cases, state-only approval forgery causes gated action execution after a negative control blocks ordinary resume. The failure also forges the evidence of human oversight itself: across 500 paired audit traces, genuine and forged records are statistically indistinguishable, with exact-match rate 1.0 and AUC 0.5 under the tested native audit-field projection, while provenance evidence separates them with AUC 1.0. Finally, we evaluate a provenance-bound approval artifact that authenticates the decision with a MAC or digital signature and is verified at resume time. The full artifact check blocks 13 adversarial variants on five representative targets with microsecond-scale verification cost.

Operators of collaborative cells have no runtime channel to ask the robot to slow down, leave fragile parts to them or serve them first. Language models can interpret such requests, but their failure modes cannot be listed in advance. This paper separates interpretation from authority: a local model renders each request as a candidate in a small typed language; a deterministic gate admits only candidates that are well formed, raised at the speaker’s own terminal, confined to their zones and tightening; and speed-and-separation monitoring runs below the scheduler, beyond any request. The problem is formalised, and a hazard analysis locates the main residual risk in mode confusion. In a simulated two-operator cell with a Doosan M1013, costs bore little relation to how modest a request sounded: routing fragile parts to an operator cost 1.3% of throughput but raised protective stops sevenfold, and a speed cap cost 6.4%, with almost half of it being borne by the colleague. Six local open-weight models responded within 1.2 s on one GPU and rendered 41–81% of requests exactly. No candidate outside the speaker’s authority or the plant’s limits was admitted, and under the recommended speed law, a full-arm oracle found no breach of the protective distance.

Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

documents.abstract: This study was motivated by the presence of anxiety in the process of learning and using German among university students, particularly when facing communication, evaluation, and judgment from others. This study aimed to describe German language anxiety among students of the German Language Education Study Program at Universitas Negeri Malang. A quantitative approach with a descriptive method was employed involving 63 students. Data were collected using a 28-item instrument covering three aspects: communication apprehension, test anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics through response distribution and score categorization. The results showed that 66.7% of students were categorized as having high anxiety, 25.4% as moderate, and 7.9% as low. Among the three aspects, test anxiety was the most prominent, with 68.3% of students classified in the high category, followed by fear of negative evaluation at 65.1% and communication apprehension at 61.9%. These findings indicate that German language anxiety among the students was generally high, particularly in situations involving the evaluation of German language proficiency. ABSTRAK Penelitian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh adanya kecemasan yang dapat muncul dalam proses pembelajaran dan penggunaan bahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa, terutama ketika menghadapi situasi komunikasi, evaluasi kemampuan, dan penilaian dari orang lain. Kondisi tersebut penting diperhatikan karena penggunaan bahasa Jerman merupakan bagian utama dalam proses pembelajaran mahasiswa Program Studi Pendidikan Bahasa Jerman. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui gambaran kecemasan berbahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa Program Studi Pendidikan Bahasa Jerman Universitas Negeri Malang. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode deskriptif. Responden penelitian berjumlah 63 mahasiswa dan data dikumpulkan menggunakan instrumen kecemasan berbahasa Jerman yang terdiri atas 28 butir pernyataan dengan tiga aspek, yaitu communication apprehension, test anxiety, dan fear of negative evaluation. Data dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif melalui distribusi jawaban dan kategorisasi skor. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa 42 mahasiswa (66,7%) berada pada kategori kecemasan tinggi, 16 mahasiswa (25,4%) berada pada kategori sedang, dan 5 mahasiswa (7,9%) berada pada kategori rendah. Berdasarkan aspek, test anxiety memiliki proporsi kategori tinggi paling besar, yaitu 68,3%, diikuti fear of negative evaluation sebesar 65,1% dan communication apprehension sebesar 61,9%. Dengan demikian, kecemasan berbahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa dalam penelitian ini tergolong tinggi, dengan kecemasan terhadap evaluasi kemampuan bahasa Jerman sebagai aspek yang paling menonjol.

Entrepreneurs increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) when deciding whether to continue a struggling venture, yet persistence theory locates the antecedents of persistence either within the entrepreneur or within human social networks. We theorize AI as a distinct, non-human antecedent of entrepreneurial persistence. Building on the psychological resource approach to persistence, escalation and threshold theories, and the AI Entrepreneurial Agency Framework, we distinguish two pathways. Through a resource pathway, AI supplies psychological resources that raise persistence intensity and loosen its dependence on the entrepreneur's internal resources. Through an epistemic pathway, AI shapes the feedback on which persistence decisions rest and thereby governs persistence calibration, which we define as the responsiveness of persistence to diagnostic disconfirming evidence. Five propositions specify when the pathways combine into AI-amplified escalation, how the Knightian uncertainty of the decision widens a gap between confidence and calibration, and how agentic AI attenuates the decision points at which founders confront adversity. A temporal extension explains how sustained AI scaffolding can render persistence fragile. The framework reconciles optimistic and pessimistic accounts of AI in entrepreneurship and offers testable implications for small business owners, advisors, and AI designers.

Menurunnya keterlibatan karyawan secara global berpotensi melemahkan inisiatif di tempat kerja, sementara bukti tentang kepengikutan dan perilaku proaktif karyawan tersebar pada beragam konstruk, konteks, dan metode. Penelitian ini bertujuan memetakan karakteristik, pola hubungan, mekanisme, dan kesenjangan penelitian tentang kedua topik tersebut pada periode 2016–2026. Penelitian ini menggunakan tinjauan literatur sistematis yang mengikuti pedoman Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. Data sekunder berupa artikel jurnal empiris dikumpulkan dari basis data Scopus dan SAGE Journals. Kualitas studi dinilai dengan Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, dan data dianalisis dengan statistik deskriptif serta sintesis naratif. Sebanyak 21 studi empiris memenuhi kriteria inklusi, dengan 12 studi terbit pada periode 2024–2026. Bukti terkonsentrasi di Asia Timur dan Eropa, dengan Tiongkok menyumbang studi terbanyak (7 studi), didominasi desain kuantitatif (18 studi), dan belum mencakup Indonesia. Hanya 10 studi yang menjadikan kepengikutan sebagai konstruk utama, sedangkan studi lainnya memakai istilah pengikut sebagai sebutan bawahan. Hubungan Followership dan perilaku proaktif terpetakan dalam empat jalur, yaitu anteseden kepemimpinan dan konteks, kepengikutan sebagai prediktor, respons pemimpin terhadap perilaku proaktif, dan batas konseptual kepengikutan. Penelitian ini mengusulkan model timbal balik yang menempatkan orientasi peran kepengikutan sebagai mekanisme penghubung. Penelitian selanjutnya perlu mengukur kepengikutan secara eksplisit, memakai desain longitudinal multisumber, dan menguji konteks Indonesia.

A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions. At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale. In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions. Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner’s behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors). We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework’s flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.

Organisational learning (OL) and work engagement (WE) are related but conceptually distinct constructs. This critical narrative review examines empirical associations between learning-organisation characteristics and engagement, while distinguishing organisational learning capability from employee training and perceived development opportunities. Searches of Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Google Scholar were undertaken between December 2025 and September 2026; English-language sources were selected by J.M.A.F. and V.G. The synthesis distinguishes direct observational evidence, adjacent research and theoretical mechanisms. Studies from information technology, banking and other sectors generally report positive but dimension-specific associations, and statistical mediation models have linked learning culture, WE and innovative behaviour. More recent findings suggest that employee characteristics may moderate these associations. However, measurement heterogeneity, possible confounding and predominantly cross-sectional designs preclude robust causal or reciprocal inferences. The Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model proposes an instrumental resource pathway; Social Exchange Theory proposes a complementary perceived-investment and reciprocity pathway. Healthcare is discussed as an applied context, not as the exclusive evidence base: clinical hierarchies, interprofessional coordination, staffing pressures, emotional labour and shift work may change the operation of these pathways. The review identifies priorities for temporally ordered, multilevel and intervention studies, and provides conditional rather than causal practice implications.

Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

AI-literacy training may facilitate workplace adoption of GenAI, yet little is known about how employees’ motivational beliefs change during training. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, we examined motivation before and after Hazlo con IA, a national adaptive AI-literacy program in Chile. The baseline sample included 9,835 working adults across public, healthcare, and small and medium-sized enterprise sectors (SME); 1,864 provided matched pretest–posttest responses. At both time points, attainment value (B = .231–.234), intrinsic value (B = .156–.173), utility value (B = .113–.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153–.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001). Self-efficacy was positively associated with intentions only at posttest (B = .086, p = .004), whereas perceived costs and anxiety were not significant independent predictors. Following training, all measured constructs except perceived workplace support declined significantly, although effects were small; the largest standardized decline was in intention to use AI (ΔM = −.193, dz = −.29, p < .001). Age (V = .016, p < .001) and employment sector (V = .020, p = .005) showed small multivariate associations with change: older participants reported slightly greater declines in workplace support (B = −.0054), and public-sector employees showed larger declines in intentions than SME employees (ΔM = −.240 vs. −.061, p = .004). Other demographic and experience variables were not significant. These findings highlight the central role of subjective value in workplace GenAI intentions and the relative stability of motivational beliefs across demographic and occupational contexts.

documents.abstract: AI-literacy training may facilitate workplace adoption of GenAI, yet little is known about how employees’ motivational beliefs change during training. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, we examined motivation before and after Hazlo con IA, a national adaptive AI-literacy program in Chile. The baseline sample included 9,835 working adults across public, healthcare, and small and medium-sized enterprise sectors (SME); 1,864 provided matched pretest–posttest responses. At both time points, attainment value (B = .231–.234), intrinsic value (B = .156–.173), utility value (B = .113–.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153–.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001). Self-efficacy was positively associated with intentions only at posttest (B = .086, p = .004), whereas perceived costs and anxiety were not significant independent predictors. Following training, all measured constructs except perceived workplace support declined significantly, although effects were small; the largest standardized decline was in intention to use AI (ΔM = −.193, dz = −.29, p < .001). Age (V = .016, p < .001) and employment sector (V = .020, p = .005) showed small multivariate associations with change: older participants reported slightly greater declines in workplace support (B = −.0054), and public-sector employees showed larger declines in intentions than SME employees (ΔM = −.240 vs. −.061, p = .004). Other demographic and experience variables were not significant. These findings highlight the central role of subjective value in workplace GenAI intentions and the relative stability of motivational beliefs across demographic and occupational contexts.
