The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) marks a turning point in language education, accelerating the shift from traditional methodologies toward AI-enhanced learning environments. The aim of this article is to examine the impact of GenAI on language education, understood not as a complementary tool but as a linguistic and epistemological disruption that transforms processes of language production, evaluation, and acquisition. Drawing on a documentary analysis that integrates recent theoretical, empirical, and regulatory sources, the study addresses four interrelated objectives: to reorganize instructional design toward generative tasks of greater cognitive complexity; to identify pedagogical applications of GenAI through tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva, HeyGen, and other emerging GenAI systems; to redefine the teacher’s role as a critical orchestrator and AI-literate professional; and to examine the ethical and linguistic challenges posed by GenAI, including hallucination, discourse homogenization, and risks to academic integrity. The findings indicate that GenAI enhances learning only when embedded within intentional, critically mediated, and well-supervised pedagogy that preserves cognitive engagement, linguistic diversity, and educational equity.[La rápida expansión de la inteligencia artificial generativa (IAGen) marca un punto de inflexión en la enseñanza de lenguas, impulsando la transición desde métodos tradicionales hacia entornos de aprendizaje enriquecidos por IA. El objetivo de este artículo es examinar el impacto de la IAGen en la enseñanza de lenguas, entendida no como una herramienta complementaria, sino como una disrupción lingüística y epistemológica que transforma los procesos de producción, evaluación y adquisición del lenguaje. Mediante un análisis documental que integra fuentes teóricas, empíricas y normativas recientes, el estudio persigue cuatro objetivos específicos: reorganizar el diseño didáctico hacia actividades generativas de mayor complejidad cognitiva; identificar formas de implementación de la IAGen a través de herramientas como ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva o HeyGen; redefinir el rol docente como orquestador crítico y profesional con alfabetización en IA; y examinar los desafíos éticos y lingüísticos derivados de la IAGen, como la alucinación, la homogeneización del discurso o los riesgos para la integridad académica. Los resultados del análisis indican que la IAGen solo mejora el aprendizaje cuando se integra en una pedagogía intencional, crítica y supervisada que preserve el compromiso cognitivo, la diversidad lingüística y la equidad educativa].

Psychosocial hazards can compromise more than worker wellbeing. In safety–critical systems, sustained workload and uncertainty can combine with reduced recovery to weaken the human and organisational capacities through which risks are recognised and controlled. This study develops a systems model of how psychosocial demands, leadership buffering, and boundary disruption can constrain sustained adaptation while operations continue. We examine these dynamics among middle-level leaders in Australia’s mining, oil, and gas sector during the prolonged COVID-19 crisis. Positioned between executive decision-making and frontline operations, these leaders translated changing directives into operating practice while carrying responsibility for continuity and employee wellbeing. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 managers and eight general managers. Team-based thematic analysis was supported by a cross-case descriptive matrix of recurring conditions. Leaders described isolation and disconnection alongside work intensification and fatigue. Persistent uncertainty was often accompanied by anxiety. As organisational arrangements changed, leadership roles expanded and work–nonwork boundaries became more permeable. Middle-level leaders buffered competing organisational and workforce demands, helping operations continue while opportunities for recovery narrowed. Participants described growing difficulty sustaining adaptive effort. The model distinguishes adaptive performance from adaptive sustainability. Continued functioning may coexist with depletion of the resources that enable further adaptation. We extend safety science by conceptualising psychosocial risk as a dynamic organisational process and identifying middle-level leaders as potential sources of safety intelligence. Effective control requires organisations to address how work itself generates exposure, including the staffing and authority available to leaders. Boundary protection and recovery should sit alongside individual support.

Background Physical education (PE) classes are intrinsically heterogeneous, yet students differing in competence, readiness, and motivation are often exposed to uniform instructional demands. Differentiated instruction has been widely advocated as a response to learner diversity, but rigorous evidence regarding its motivational consequences and underlying psychological processes remains limited. Methods We conducted a two-arm cluster-randomized longitudinal trial across 12 secondary schools in Zhengzhou, China. Forty-eight teacher–class clusters comprising 1,152 students aged 12–15 years were randomized to a 12-week differentiated-instruction intervention or usual PE. The intervention systematically adapted task challenge, instructional support, grouping, pacing, progression, and bounded choice to students’ readiness and learning needs. Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), during intervention (T1), post-intervention (T2), and follow-up (T3). The primary outcome was autonomous motivation at T2; secondary outcomes were psychological need satisfaction and frustration, controlled motivation, amotivation, and PE engagement. Three-level longitudinal mixed-effects models and multilevel longitudinal mediation models were used. Results At T2, differentiated instruction produced higher autonomous motivation than usual PE (adjusted difference = 0.49, 95% CI [0.39, 0.59]; standardized effect = 0.72). It also increased psychological need satisfaction (0.53, 95% CI [0.41, 0.65]) and PE engagement (0.46, 95% CI [0.37, 0.55]), while reducing psychological need frustration (−0.46, 95% CI [−0.57, −0.35]) and amotivation (−0.38, 95% CI [−0.47, −0.29]); effects on controlled motivation were small. Longitudinal mediation was consistent with two complementary pathways: greater T1 need satisfaction was associated with higher T2 autonomous motivation (indirect effect β = 0.13, 95% CI [0.09, 0.18]), whereas lower T1 need frustration was associated with lower T2 amotivation (indirect effect β = −0.11, 95% CI [−0.15, −0.07]). Several effects remained evident at T3, although attenuated. Conclusion Differentiated instruction improved motivational functioning in PE by reshaping the instructional conditions through which students experienced challenge, support, progression, and participation. The findings extend differentiated-instruction research beyond pedagogical adaptation by identifying instructional design as a motivationally relevant component of the PE environment and by supporting complementary need-satisfaction and need-frustration pathways linking differentiated instruction with autonomous motivation and amotivation.

As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Appropriate reliance on autonomy in multi-agent systems requires operators to continuously evaluate and assign leadership among heterogeneous autonomous agents as task demands and environmental conditions evolve. Research on human-autonomy collaboration has demonstrated promise for anticipated situations and dyadic interactions, but lacks investigation into how operators calibrate trust and competence assessments to support dynamic leadership assignment across multiple agents during unanticipated events. This study investigates temporal modeling of human leadership assignment to multiple autonomous agents based on real-time trust and competence assessment in multi-agent systems. Thirty-nine participants completed three simulated search-and-rescue scenarios involving four autonomous uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). Each scenario was comprised of twenty object identification trials. Participants rated trust and ranked competence for each UAV in every trial. Results revealed that participants assigned leadership to UAVs based on both competence and trust assessments with respect to the task and environmental conditions. Participants’ assignment performance improved across successive scenarios as they gained experience with UAV capabilities. Network representations of trust, competence and leadership assignment, termed Trust-Competence-Identity-Networks (TCIN), were constructed for every trial and modeled sequentially using Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (TERGM) to examine the temporal evolution of human perception and leadership assignment (i.e., UAV reliance). TERGM results indicated that trust reflects personalized assessments developed through interaction experience, while competence represents task-specific assessments for leadership assignment. This research extends reliance research on dyadic interactions to multi-agent interactions, introduces the TCIN for studying leadership or reliance dynamics, and provides practical insights for designing adaptive multi-agent systems.

Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.

Context: In this chapter, the implementation and governance of User-Centered Design (UCD) are analyzed.At present, organizations are adopting the international principles of the ISO 9241-210 standard and moving away from linear software and hardware development schemes.The standard adopts a constructivist approach that places human needs and capabilities at the center of the sociotechnical cycle of technology.Objective: The purpose of the study is to set out the normative epistemology of ISO 9241-210, to distinguish analytically between user-centered and human-centered design, and to describe what the iterative operational cycle consists of, together with the techniques of empirical measurement and participatory co-design.Method: A theoretical-descriptive documentary review was carried out on the basis of international criteria in ergonomics, psychophysical methods for interface evaluation, and co-creation dynamics for information architectures.Results: The findings indicate that iterating through the operational cycle, together with quantitative techniques such as eye-tracking and the SUS and UMUX scales, prevents both the aesthetic trap and cognitive overload.Nevertheless, challenges persist, such as the management of multidisciplinary teams and the reduction of the complex human being to purely instrumental roles.Conclusions: Through cyclical and participatory iteration, companies obtain an auditable process that lowers the costs of subsequent corrective redesign.It is advisable for collaborative design practices to be institutionalized in order to strengthen usability and the reflective dimension of the brand.

Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

Human oversight is widely prescribed for high-impact artificial intelligence, but “human in the loop” is not an operational policy when review capacity is finite and agent activity varies over time. We formulate oversight for financial AI agents as a capacity-constrained allocation problem: for each proposed action, a controller decides whether to permit automated execution or consume scarce human review. Unlike a preliminary version of this study, risk scores are not drawn conditional on the realized outcome: observable features are generated first, harm is a hidden logistic function of those features, and a logistic-regression risk model is fit on a separate 60-day, 14,264-action calibration stream, then frozen and evaluated out-of-sample on a held-out 120-day, 28,174-action test stream across five financial domains. The frozen model is well calibrated out of sample (test Brier score 0.091; predicted/observed decile harm rates agree within 1–2 points). We compare no review, random review, a calibration-frozen threshold (uncapped and capacity-truncated), daily risk ranking, a convex risk-severity heuristic, and a genuine expected-loss policy selecting marginal-benefit-maximizing cases under the model’s own optimality argument. The uncapped threshold captures 40.9% of harm value but breaches the 33-action daily capacity on 49 of 120 days; truncating it recovers feasibility at a coverage cost (36.9%). Under the hard constraint, risk ranking captures 38.9% of harm value; the expected-loss policy raises this to 45.5% (a 17% relative gain) and achieves the lowest total expected cost among all evaluated policies, 10.2% below risk ranking at the same 14.1% review rate, while random allocation captures only 13.2%. A 27-cell factorial sensitivity analysis over reviewer effectiveness, review cost, and score discrimination, plus a sweep over harm prevalence and severity dispersion, shows this advantage is stable throughout. Results are computed outputs of the stated synthetic simulation; harm prevention is evaluated in expectation via the assumed reviewer-effectiveness parameter, not observed human-review outcomes. These results show that effective human oversight is jointly a prediction, allocation, and workforce-capacity problem: calibrated risk scores alone are insufficient, and unconstrained cost optimization can redistribute review away from low-severity domains.

documents.abstract: As generative AI enters creative work, practitioners must decide where AI assistance ends and human authorship begins. Human-agent interaction (HAI) research has examined AI as a tool, collaborator, consultant, and competitor. The longitudinal problem is how these roles are revised as systems become more capable, public, and economically embedded. We report a five-year interview study with 17 Chinese digital painters, based on annual semi-structured interviews from 2021 to 2025. Participants described recurring but non-uniform patterns of protective resistance, pragmatic task delegation, and, for some, reflective agency repartitioning. Early resistance protected observation, originality, signature, and ownership from AI. Later delegation placed AI in bounded tasks such as references, backgrounds, rough sketches, and client-facing drafts. By 2025, some participants built hybrid workflows around human-only zones, while others described fatigue, precarity, or difficulty locating a remaining human role. Peer norms, emotional climates, and production pressures shaped which delegations felt useful, acceptable, or exhausting. Copyright, authorship, and creative labor remained recurring limits on what participants were willing to delegate. We frame these accounts as longitudinal agency partitioning, the situated work of deciding which stages, responsibilities, values, and claims remain human in creative human-agent interaction. We discuss design implications for revisable agency-boundary controls, provenance scaffolds, and community-facing authorship norms.

documents.abstract: As conversational AI tools like ChatGPT become increasingly integrated into education, concerns have emerged about how negative information (linguistic cues emphasizing uncertainty, difficulty, or risk) may influence adolescents’ trust and learning behaviors. This study examined associations between negative ChatGPT responses, adolescents’ AI distrust, and learning-related outcomes, including motivation and discontinuation. Among 250 adolescents aged 12–13 who completed a 10-minute ChatGPT-based learning activity on inductive and deductive reasoning, analyses of 195 participants indicated that greater frequency of and initial exposure to negative information were associated with higher AI distrust, which was related to lower learning motivation and greater learning discontinuation. Moreover, dissatisfaction with ChatGPT’s responses moderated these relationships, such that associations between AI distrust and lower learning motivation and greater learning discontinuation were stronger among more dissatisfied adolescents. These findings underscore the importance of how negative AI-generated information is communicated, given its potential implications for adolescents’ trust, motivation, and continued learning engagement.

The writing task in Test for English Majors Grade Eight (TEM-8) places high demands on learners’ ability to synthesize information and express critical perspectives. Drawing on teaching practice in the English Writing and Translating Skills Training course for English majors at a Double First-Class agricultural university, this study develops a four-tier model of AI-enhanced writing instruction, with the four tiers corresponding to four ascending levels of cognitive engagement: evaluative regulation, critical analysis, comparative discernment, and selective revision. Using ChatGPT and DeepSeek as supporting tools, the model treats AI as a tool for cognitive enhancement rather than a substitute writer. By analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of AI-generated essays, comparing outputs from different platforms, and using AI critically to revise their own work, students make a cognitive shift from passively receiving feedback to actively directing their use of the technology. This paper explains the rationale, key components, and implementation of the model, offering a replicable framework for integrating AI into writing instruction for English majors in higher education.

Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

documents.abstract: Algorithmically mediated work systems are reshaping how organizations govern workers’ time. This paper develops the Temporal Sociotechnical Algorithmic Model (TSAM), a sociological theory explaining how computationally mediated information asymmetries alter workers’ capacity to anticipate, allocate, withhold, and collectively contest their labor time. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of 56 peer-reviewed publications identified through a structured search covering 2000–2024, TSAM begins from a generative condition in which labor time becomes an optimizable organizational resource while workers retain only partial visibility into the processes governing allocation, availability, and evaluation. From this condition, the model specifies three system-level mechanisms: unpredictability, latency compression, and temporal opacity. It distinguishes these mechanisms from temporal anticipatory compliance, an emergent behavioral adaptation through which workers reorganize their availability, responsiveness, and temporal boundaries in anticipation of uncertain consequences. By integrating labor process theory, the sociology of time, and sociotechnical systems theory, TSAM explains how computational mediation reconfigures the informational and temporal conditions through which control is exercised, experienced, and contested. The model further theorizes why resource-protective behavior may become less effective when reduced availability carries uncertain consequences, conceptualizes temporal opacity as epistemic asymmetry rather than simple information deficit, and positions resistance as mechanism-specific modification of algorithmic temporal governance. Five propositions translate these theoretical claims into empirically testable and refutable expectations.

documents.abstract: The mining industry is dangerous, with all these accidents happening even though safety rules have gotten better over time. It leads to real tragedies, like people dying on the job. This necessitates adopting advanced Total Quality Management (TQM) practices. This study aims to reduce fatalities by implementing a Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA) methodology within the organization to enhance occupational health and safety performance. We gathered data from questionnaires handed out to actual miners, focusing on what causes these deadly accidents, and used a tree diagram as a strategic framework for designing safety interventions and identifying learning pathways. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pareto charts to prioritize high-risk activities. The survey findings suggest that management and leadership commitment, safety training and competency, and safety culture were perceived by respondents as the most important factors influencing safety performance, collectively contributing 61.8% of the impact on safety-related activities. After applying a fishbone diagram analysis, human factors and inadequate maintenance schedules were identified as critical root causes. Overall, The study proposes a PDSA approach to improve Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) performance through TQM practices. For improving OSH performance and illustrates its potential application through hypothetical performance indicators. Due to the exploratory nature of the study and the limited sample size, further empirical validation using real operational data is required.

Mental workload is one of the main ergonomic risks in today's administrative environments, where psychosocial demands predominate. The objective of this research was to comparatively analyze the mental workload levels of the administrative staff at the Faculty of Engineering of the National University of Chimborazo (UNACH) using the NASA-TLX and SWAT methods, and to determine their relationship with sociodemographic variables. A quantitative, descriptive-correlational, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted with the entire administrative staff (n = 10). Data were processed in SPSS V26 using the chi-square test and Cramér's V coefficient. The results showed a predominance of high mental workload in both instruments (NASA-TLX: 90.0%; SWAT: 60.0%); no statistically significant relationship was found with age or years of experience. These results highlight the importance of implementing psychosocial intervention measures.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly enters human professional domains , understanding emotional reactions to its involvement becomes critical . We introduce a novel experimental paradigm that distinguishes between AI involvement in “Thinker” and “Doer” roles to examine how the role AI occupies shapes affective and evaluative responses to human–AI collaboration . Across four countries ( N = 1,345), including the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and Colombia, participants evaluated scenarios in which professional jobs were completed under four conditions: human only, full AI automation, human as Thinker with AI as Doer, or AI as Thinker with human as Doer. Our results showed that AI involvement decreased positive affect and appreciation while increasing negative affect . We also found particularly negative emotional reactions to AI executing emotionally charged professions (e.g., artist). Individual differences in AI anthropomorphism consistently moderated these effects. These findings demonstrate that emotional reactions to AI depend on the role it plays and the domain in which it operates. This research highlights the importance of task characteristics and individual differences in understanding human–AI collaboration in professional settings.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in decisions that affect health, safety, welfare and rights, and regulators have responded by requiring “control safeguards”, such as human oversight, robustness and monitoring, for systems classed as high-risk. This article asks why such safeguards are hard to implement and why the difficulty matters for society. It combines doctrinal analysis of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended in 2026) with a structured critical review of the technical, human-factors and policy literature. Five technical barriers are identified (model opacity, speed and autonomy, brittle guardrails, limits of human attention and judgement, and the lack of tests for control effectiveness), together with six legal and institutional barriers (open-textured legal standards, uncertain classification, delayed standards and guidance, limited regulatory capacity, fragmented enforcement, and burdens on small organisations). The article argues that these barriers reinforce one another through three gaps: a feasibility gap between what the law demands and what technology can deliver, a verification gap between legal requirements and testable criteria, and a capacity gap between large and small actors and between providers and regulators. Mapping each oversight capability in Article 14(4) to these barriers shows where safeguards are most likely to be formal rather than effective. The article proposes ten recommendations for EU institutions, standard-setters, national authorities, providers and deployers, and considers lessons for lower-capacity jurisdictions, including in Africa, that are drawing on EU-style models. The central conclusion is that regulatory attention should shift from documenting oversight to demonstrating that it works.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support learning and emotion regulation, yet frequent or coping-oriented use does not necessarily constitute difficult-to-regulate dependency. It remains unclear how academic rumination and affective coping are positioned relative to dependency and whether dependency is differentially associated with perceived costs to knowledge internalization and independent reasoning. This study examined these distinctions within a single educational psychology model. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 611 current GenAI users recruited through university settings in Tianjin, China (91.7% first-year students). Dependency was a continuous, nonclinical tendency. Ordinal CFA and WLSMV SEM evaluated a prespecified partial association model. Covariate adjustment, four alternative measurement specifications, an AR-score hybrid, and observed-score regressions assessed sensitivity. Results In the reference model, academic rumination was associated with affective coping (β = 0.283), and both were associated with dependency (β = 0.187 and 0.555). Dependency was associated with perceived internalization/memory debt (β = 0.550) and independent-reasoning debt (β = 0.644); their standardized difference was 0.095 (95% Monte Carlo CI [0.032, 0.157]). The corresponding observed-score coefficients were 0.413 and 0.518, with a difference of 0.105 (95% bootstrap CI [0.035, 0.175]). Both serial coefficient products remained positive, but the negative conditional coping-internalization association was not sustained in the observed-score analysis. Reported frequency had no unique association in the combined adjusted model. Alternative measurement models retained robust RMSEA of 0.090–0.097; robust hybrid indices were unavailable. Conclusion The results provide tentative evidence of differentiated self-reported associations among coping, frequency, dependency, and cognitive concerns. Measurement misfit remains unresolved, and the coping-outcome coefficients were sensitive to construct representation. Observed-score consistency for dependency and serial products does not validate the latent structure or establish temporal or causal mediation. These predominantly first-year, Tianjin-based cross-sectional data do not establish objective cognitive decline or generality across student populations.

We propose co-creative learning as a novel paradigm where biological and artificial agents (e.g. humans and robots) mutually integrate their partial perceptual information and knowledge to construct shared external representations, a process we interpret as symbol emergence. Unlike traditional AI teaching based on unilateral knowledge transfer, this addresses the challenge of integrating information from inherently different modalities. We empirically test this framework using a Human–AI interaction model based on the Metropolis-Hastings naming game (MHNG), a decentralized Bayesian inference mechanism. In an online experiment, 69 participants played a joint attention naming game (JA-NG) with one of three computer agent types (MH-based, always-accept, or always-reject) under partial observability. Results show that Human–AI pairs improved their categorization accuracy through interaction, and that an MH-based agent converged on a shared sign system aligned with the two agents' joint observations significantly more closely than an agent learning from its own observations alone, a process underpinned by the collaborative minimization of their collective free energy. No statistically significant difference between the MH and Always Accept conditions was detected after Holm correction. Unlike unconditional acceptance under Always Accept, however, the MH-based agent uses an evidence-sensitive acceptance rule based on its local generative model. Furthermore, human acceptance behavior aligned closely with the MH-derived acceptance probability. These findings provide the first empirical evidence for co-creative learning emerging in Human–AI dyads via MHNG-based interaction. This suggests a promising path toward symbiotic AI systems that learn with humans, rather than from them, by dynamically aligning perceptual experiences, opening a new venue for symbiotic and organic AI alignment.

Avatars serve as virtual representations of users in digital environments. Their appearance can be freely customized, often leading to discrepancies between visual representation and the user's real identity. Such appearances may unconsciously influence interpersonal trust, complicating the assessment of trustworthiness in virtual interactions. To investigate how avatar characteristics influence trust, we developed and preliminarily validated the Avatar Trust Scale (ATS), a tool designed to quantify trust specifically in the context of avatars. Based on data from a German sample of 840 participants, our findings suggest a two-factor structure: Specific Trust (trustworthiness, security, and willingness to interact) and General Trust (propensity to trust avatars and humans, and avatar literacy). The scale was validated using questionnaire data and behavioral tasks (i.e., trust game, dictator game, ultimatum game). Participants interacted with a virtual agent rather than a user-controlled avatar, providing initial validation in a controlled context and laying the groundwork for future research on avatar-mediated trust.

Corporate crises are increasingly shaped by interconnected digital infrastructures, global supply chains, cloud services, artificial intelligence and data-intensive business models. This conceptual article examines how digital transformation is changing the character and management of corporate crises. It develops an integrated Digital Crisis Resilience Framework (DCRF). Drawing on crisis management, organisational resilience, dynamic capabilities, stakeholder and socio-technical systems theories, the article conceptualises resilience as a continuous strategic capability rather than a reactive emergency function. The DCRF integrates eight capabilities across the crisis lifecycle. Comparative analysis of the NotPetya/Maersk, SolarWinds, COVID-19, Colonial Pipeline and CrowdStrike cases illuminates the Digital Resilience Paradox: digitalisation can simultaneously strengthen adaptive capacity and increase systemic vulnerability. A five-level Digital Crisis Resilience Maturity Model, research propositions and an implementation roadmap are proposed. The article contributes by integrating fragmented research streams and extending crisis resilience from the firm level to the wider digital ecosystem.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Modern human–autonomy teams (HATs) often operate under time constraints that limit individuals’ ability to fully evaluate recommendations from the automation and autonomous systems. In these settings, people may rely not only on their own interactions with autonomy, but also on cues from their teammates. This study examines how decision time constraints influence trust propagation in multi-operator, multi-autonomy (MOMA) teams. Participants worked in pairs with two drones in a repeated threat-detection task, making rapid decisions under either standard (3.0 s) or constrained (1.7 s) time conditions. After each round, participants reported their trust in both drones and their teammate, allowing us to quantify how trust propagates based on teammate-reported trust. Results show that trust propagates between teammates in both conditions ( p < . 001), with stronger effects under tighter time constraints (3.0 s: b = 0.29; 1.7 s: b = 0.35). These findings highlight the role of social influences on trust in time-constrained environments and inform the design of human–autonomy systems for high-tempo operations.

Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in sub-Saharan Africa face barriers to contraceptive access and lack decision-support resources tailored to their needs. Many Kenyan AGYW seek contraceptive services in the pharmacy setting, but experience stigma, judgment, and privacy concerns that make it difficult to seek guidance from pharmacists. This work examines how chatbots could integrate into Kenya’s pharmacy setting to support AGYW’s contraceptive decision-making. We presented chatbot prototypes in co-design workshops with AGYW and pharmacy workers to evoke reflections on perceived opportunities, concerns, and preferable futures of chatbot-supported care. Our findings highlight expectations that a chatbot could offer private, non-judgmental spaces for information seeking while shifting trust and authority away from pharmacists, revealing tensions surrounding the distribution of authority, reliance, and control among AGYW, pharmacists, and the chatbot. In response to these tensions, we contribute design guidelines for chatbots to navigate community beliefs and promote shared decision-making by AGYW and pharmacists. More broadly, this work extends research on sensitive health chatbots for youth by showing how such tools embedded within a service delivery setting surface distinct considerations for stakeholder roles and person-centered care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The increasing deployment of collaborative robots (cobots) in industrial settings requires a nuanced understanding of their impact on workers.Unlike traditional automation that replaces human tasks, cobots are designed to complement and enhance human capabilities.This study reports a human-centered investigation within the MAGICIAN project, which develops cobot-supported defect detection and repair for automotive manufacturing.Fieldwork at Tofaş in Türkiye combined structured observations of eight workers across Bodyshop and Press settings, 31 stakeholder interviews, and unweighted NASA-TLX assessments with 27 workers.We detail how observational records, stakeholder accounts, and workload patterns were triangulated and translated into traceable requirements.Results identify high temporal and effort demands, distinct workload profiles between production areas, reliance on tacit visual and tactile expertise, and the importance of predictability, worker control, and integration with existing reporting practices.This work contributes to an empirically grounded requirements-elicitation framework, and a transparent, confidence-aware cobot architecture that preserves human oversight while reducing repetitive physical and cognitive strain.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly part of everyday life, yet there is no established way to measure how users evaluate their trustworthiness. This study introduces the Perceived Trustworthiness of LLMs scale (PT-LLM-8), a self-report psychometric instrument measuring users’ perceived trustworthiness of their primary LLM. PT-LLM-8 is developed from the TrustLLM framework and adapted as a human-centred measure. The PT-LLM-8 comprises eight items representing truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, transparency, accountability, and compliance with laws. Psychometric properties of the scale were tested with 752 LLM users in the United Kingdom (Mean age = 28.58, SD = 6.11, 50.3% males, 48.8% females). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a one-factor structure, with high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.90, Composite Reliability = 0.91, strong item-total correlations (ranged between 0.62 and 0.75), and measurement invariance across gender. The total score measures overall perceived trustworthiness, while individual item responses may also be examined descriptively for information about the content represented by each item. For researchers, practitioners, and developers, the PT-LLM-8 offers a practical instrument for evaluating interventions, comparing groups and contexts, and examining whether technical safeguards are reflected in users’ perceived trustworthiness of LLM. The scale can also be applied to guide system design, support policy development, and help organisations monitor shifts in user trust toward LLMs over time, making it applicable across research, practice, and governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Este artigo analisa o significado de educar em uma sociedade caracterizada pela abundância, pela velocidade e pela competição entre fontes de informação. Parte-se do problema de que ampliar o acesso a conteúdos não equivale a ampliar conhecimento, compreensão ou capacidade de julgamento. O objetivo é discutir como as instituições educacionais podem articular repertório de conhecimentos, alfabetização midiática e informacional, avaliação de fontes, raciocínio sobre evidências e uso responsável de tecnologias digitais para formar sujeitos capazes de decidir em ambientes de incerteza informacional. Metodologicamente, desenvolve-se um ensaio teórico de natureza bibliográfica e analítica, sustentado por literatura verificada sobre sobrecarga informacional, carga cognitiva, pensamento crítico, desordem informacional, raciocínio cívico on-line, intervenções de alfabetização midiática e educação digital, complementada por documentos normativos brasileiros e por marcos de organismos internacionais. A análise indica que o desafio contemporâneo não consiste em substituir a transmissão de conhecimentos por competências genéricas, mas em reorganizar a relação entre conhecimento acumulado e práticas de verificação. Argumenta-se que o julgamento crítico depende simultaneamente de saber substantivo, de critérios epistemológicos e de rotinas de investigação que permitam identificar autoria, comparar fontes, examinar evidências, reconhecer incertezas e revisar conclusões. Propõe-se, ao final, uma matriz de formação epistemológica com sete dimensões, acompanhada de uma progressão formativa e de implicações avaliativas, aplicável a diferentes níveis e modalidades de ensino, incluindo o tratamento da inteligência artificial generativa como objeto de verificação e não como autoridade epistêmica.

With the continuous advancement of artificial intelligence applications in the field of pet healthcare, AI pet medical platforms have gradually become important tools for pet health management. However, in contexts characterized by high emotional involvement and high uncertainty, users’ trust in and adoption of such platforms still face significant challenges. Based on trust calibration theory, uncertainty management theory, and the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, this study adopts a 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design to examine the effects of mimicry style (anthropomorphic design versus zoomorphic design), identity positioning (expert-authoritative versus friendly-companion), and description style (lay terminology versus professional terminology) on users’ cognitive trust, affective attachment, and usage intention. A total of 400 valid samples were collected, and the hypotheses were tested using analysis of variance and mediation analysis. The results indicate that zoomorphic design significantly enhances affective attachment and usage intention and exerts a partial mediating effect on usage intention through affective attachment and cognitive trust. Expert-authoritative identity positioning significantly increases cognitive trust and usage intention, whereas the mediating role of affective attachment is not significant. Descriptive style shows no significant direct effect on usage intention, but professional terminology exerts a mediating effect on usage intention through cognitive trust. In addition, a significant interaction effect is found between mimicry style and identity positioning. The findings suggest that user adoption of AI pet medical platforms is jointly driven by both affective and cognitive pathways, with cognitive trust playing a more central role in high-risk decision-making contexts. This study extends the application of the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm and trust calibration theory in the pet healthcare context and provides practical implications for the interface and communication design of AI pet medical platforms.

This article addresses the critical issues associated with maritime cyber-security and focusses on the training and education needed for maritime sector employees and professionals in the port sector. It provides essential context for understanding the increasing threat landscape, exemplified by a 900 per cent rise in cyber breaches targeting operational technology in ships and ports in 2023. It underscores the global impact of cyber threats, and highlights major incidents in ports worldwide. The escalating frequency of attacks on shipping lines, container terminals and national key points raises concerns about financial losses and potential risks to human life, alongside damage to infrastructure and the environment. We argue that the critical aspect of cyber resilience is the human factor, which is considered to be a potential weak link in cyber-security. We explore the importance of training the maritime workforce to enhance cyber resilience, analyse the scope of the training obligations imposed by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code, and note gaps in the application of this framework in South Africa's Merchant Shipping (Maritime Security) Regulations, 2004. Furthermore, the non-mandatory guidelines to the ISPS Code lack both force of law and sufficient specificity. Against this background we emphasise the growing attention by regulators in the United States, European Union and United Kingdom to the vulnerabilities of cyber-physical systems in ports, and the need for specific regulations to address these risks. While acknowledging the existing regulations, we advocate the urgent development of a comprehensive port-sector cyber-security policy and guidelines in South Africa and the amendment of the existing regulations to include mandatory cyber-security provisions. In conclusion we emphasise the need for a coordinated effort in the South African port sector to promote cyber resiliency, understood as being the ability to identify, mitigate and respond to cyber threats effectively. We call for the integration of cyber-security into executive strategies, policies and procedures, and stress the importance of continuous learning and information sharing to create a resilient maritime industry.

Demotivation can undermine students’ engagement and persistence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly during the transition to university, when first-year students encounter new academic and assessment demands. Understanding its sources is therefore important for supporting students’ adjustment and sustained engagement in English learning. The current study aimed to investigate the level of students’ demotivation in English learning, the dominant factors, and the differences based on gender and educational background. It focused on first-year students enrolled in an Islamic University in Madura that considers English as a compulsory and intensive course. This study was a quantitative research with a survey design. Demotivation questionnaires were adopted and modified from Sakai and Kikuchi (2009) and administered to 147 students through Google Forms. The findings revealed a moderate level of demotivation. Based on the reverse scale, in which lower scores indicate higher demotivation, test scores emerged as the most prominent demotivating factor (M = 3.03), followed by inadequate learning facilities (M = 3.16), learning contents and materials (M = 3.31), lack of intrinsic motivation (M = 3.33), and teacher competence and teaching styles (M = 3.50). A significant gender difference was found, with male students reporting higher demotivation (M = 3.10) than female students (M = 3.39), t(145) = 2.134, p = .035. In contrast, no significant difference was found across educational backgrounds, F(5, 141) = 1.068, p = .381. These findings highlight the importance of assessment experiences in first-year EFL demotivation and suggest the need for more supportive assessment practices during students’ transition to university English learning..

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now produce, within minutes, a venture risk assessment that reads like the work of an experienced analyst. Whether founders, and the investors who read their documents, can still tell how much such an assessment rests on is an open question with consequences for entrepreneurship, finance and the governance of AI. This article develops a theory of cue–evidence decoupling. People judge the strength of evidence from cues such as fluency, structure and agreement, and generative AI supplies these cues whether or not the evidence is there. Because founders act when the uncertainty they perceive falls to a level they can accept, decoupling lowers perceived uncertainty without lowering actual uncertainty. It also weakens written venture materials as costly signals to investors. Because feedback in entrepreneurship is slow and noisy, founders should learn to correct for decoupling only slowly. To make the theory testable before outcomes are known, the article draws on risk science to define the knowledge-strength gap: the number of strength-of-knowledge criteria on which a founder rates an AI-assisted risk assessment as better supported than blind raters judge a normalised version of it to be. Eight propositions specify when the gap widens (novel ventures; estimating rather than listing risks), when it narrows (an AI critic; feedback on past estimates), how it raises resource commitment and how disclosure of AI use shifts investors' errors. Each proposition is paired with a randomised test and a result that would refute it. The theory implies that AI may mislead founders most where they need it most. It recasts the debate on AI and Knightian uncertainty as a question about founders' beliefs, and it suggests that safeguards for AI-assisted decisions, including transparency rules, should target the grounds of confidence and not only the accuracy of AI output.

In higher education, agentic AI goes beyond drafting content to creating learning management system (LMS) artefacts and scheduling releases under teacher oversight. Adoption research has modelled intention towards tools that draft rather than act, leaving delegation to a system that acts unobserved. This study estimated the effect of assignment to an action-taking scenario on teachers’ workflow choices, using Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory to explain delegation within that scenario. We randomly assigned 290 university teachers to a GenAI drafting-only condition (n = 140) or an LMS-integrated agentic condition (n = 150); each made step-by-step choices in a scenario-based six-step quiz workflow combining content drafting with student-facing platform actions. Teachers assigned to the agentic scenario chose AI support for more steps (d = 0.65), but the gain sat almost entirely on content drafting (d = 0.99) and was negligible for platform actions (d = 0.12). This content–platform boundary was sharp: 92% chose to delegate question writing, while 77% chose to schedule releases manually. Most chose limited autonomy (48% selected draft-only, 35% selected approval-gated publishing, 5% selected auto-publish). The five DOI attributes and controls explained substantial variance in an Agentic Use Behaviour Index (AUBI) of delegation, autonomy, and permissions (R2 = 0.65). Complexity, understood as oversight burden, was negatively associated with AUBI, and its association with non-manual engagement was stronger in the agentic scenario; observability was not significant. The direction of the AUBI results held across four weightings and count and ordinal models, and exploratory clustering suggested four adopter profiles forming a permission ladder. Extending DOI from tool adoption to task delegation, the results favour draft-first defaults, approval gates, and staged permissions, with field replication using LMS logs a priority.

Non-academic tutoring is an important channel through which families help their children accumulate cultural capital. Existing studies have mostly analysed parental motivations from a static perspective, and few have examined how students' motivations change across educational stages. Based on in-depth interviews with 22 art-track candidates, this article finds that their motivations for participating in arts tutoring show a marked shift from value rationality to instrumental rationality. In primary school and before, the intrinsic motivation of personal interest dominated their participation in interest classes. At the two key educational transitions of the high school entrance examination (zhongkao) and the college entrance examination (gaokao), they chose to study art majors out of the extrinsic motivation of examination progression. In this process, the form of tutoring they attended shifted from arts interest classes to professional intensive training classes, and the learning content was replaced by examination subjects for art majors.

Background Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in bilingual education is increasingly consequential for students' cognitive engagement and professional communication, yet prior research has examined these outcomes largely in isolation. Whether learning engagement and cross-cultural competence (CCC) operate as simultaneous, parallel indirect pathways linking AI integration to perceived learning effectiveness and business communication skill remains underexamined, and cultural intelligence has rarely been modeled as a boundary condition on the intercultural pathway. Methods Drawing on a cross-sectional dataset of 604 bilingual education students across 13 universities in China, this study integrated the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Social Cognitive Theory, and Cultural Intelligence Theory within a single framework. Ordinary least squares regression with HC3 robust standard errors and partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrap-based indirect effect and latent moderation analyses were employed. Results All three indirect pathways were statistically supported: AI → learning engagement → perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.191), AI → CCC → business communication skill (β = 0.278), and AI → CCC → perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.202), each carrying a larger share of the AI-outcome association than the corresponding direct path. The model explained 28.38% of variance in learning engagement, 34.33% in CCC, 40.85% in business communication skill, and 47.28% in perceived learning effectiveness. Cultural intelligence positively moderated the AI → CCC association (β = 0.200), with simple slopes rising from 0.298 at low cultural intelligence to 0.697 at high cultural intelligence. Conclusion AI integration is associated with distal learning and communication outcomes predominantly through engagement-related and intercultural mechanisms, with cultural intelligence conditioning the strength of the intercultural pathway. These findings suggest that AI funding in bilingual education should be conditioned on process metrics, learning engagement and intercultural capability, rather than on tool procurement alone. Structured intercultural scaffolding should be required as an accreditation condition for AI-supported bilingual courses, and cultural intelligence screening at program entry with tiered support for lower-cultural-intelligence learners warrants consideration, given that the benefits of AI-supported learning are non-uniform across learners.

Faster information processing does not necessarily leave a manufacturing firm better prepared for disruption. This conceptual article examines how generative artificial intelligence affects operational resilience in Chinese manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises. A theory synthesis connects organizational memory with research on human–automation interaction, using published workplace evidence to distinguish established findings from proposed mechanisms. The resulting framework identifies two competing pathways. AI-assisted documentation can make operational experience available to other employees, while repeated delegation can reduce the independent competence needed when assistance fails. Five propositions specify how retention procedures, domain expertise, decision authority, disruption novelty, and fallback capacity affect these pathways. The contribution is a process-level explanation of why routine productivity and disruption performance can move in different directions, rather than a claim that AI adoption inherently produces resilience. A proposed factorial study separates the effects of AI access from those of knowledge-management practices. For managers, the framework supports selective documentation, decisions matched to available verification, and continuity exercises that test both records and employee competence.

Through interviews and questionnaires, we investigate geoscience students’ motivations, expectations and concerns at the start of the bachelor programme at the University of Oslo, Norway, and how these change as the students encounter the courses, peers, staff and study environment in their first year. Students begin with a mix of extrinsic and intrinsic motivations that become more self-determined over the first year. Initially, they are eager to learn but unsure they can succeed; by year’s end doubts shift toward the applicability of their education and future job prospects. Students hope to build relationships and make friends and fear that they will not; although these fears subside quickly for most, students consistently emphasize the importance of positive relationships. Though greater self-determination and better relationships typically are viewed as something positive, for some students it appears that increased self-determination is accompanied by heightened sensitivity to academic difficulties, teacher expectations, and the implications of success or failure. Though institutional shortcomings were not cited as reasons for dropping out by participants in this study, the findings highlight opportunities to support student success and retention by addressing self-efficacy, study technique, perceived relevance, and workload management.

Bluesky, a novel social networking platform, offers a space with valuable community ties for transfeminine individuals. At the same time, though, these communities are not free of intracommunity conflict, particularly conflict predicated on a transmisogynistic politics of disposability. We conduct a grounded theory interview study with 13 transfeminine Bluesky users, finding that transfeminine individuals experience attacks predicated on their disposability that are primarily driven by a form of disinformation we call distributed, consensus-free (DCF) folklore. DCF folklore turns communities against users who have previously provided crucial labor to those same communities; we frame it as an networked phenomenon that results from extant dynamics and affordances on the platform. In order to mitigate the harms done by the circulation of this folklore, we conclude by discussing opportunities for tools to more effectively support bottom-up moderation that affords for nuance and contextualization.

Purpose: The study aimed to assess the mediating effect of trust and task-technology fit in human-AI collaboration environments in employee engagement in digital workplaces. Design/methodology/approach: A mixed-methods study design was used with 687 employees in various industries. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test the relationships among the capabilities of the AI system, trust, and task-technology fit, as well as relationships between employee engagement and trust. 42 participants in qualitative interviews gave further insights into the interaction patterns between humans and AI. Results: The results show that the capabilities of AI systems substantially contribute to employee engagement via their role of full mediation, namely through their mediation by trust in AI systems (indirect effect = 0.31, p < 0.001) and task-technology fit (indirect effect = 0.27, p < 0.001). The indirect effects of AI Design Quality in the mediation model through trust (0.32) and task-technology fit (0.29) are comparable, resulting in total effects of β = 0.66, p < 0.001. The study shows that design and customization of AI are key factors in boosting employee trust and engagement, and transparency is key to this. Research limitations/implications: Because this was a cross-sectional study, causal inferences are limited. Longitudinal research is needed to investigate the dynamic nature of human-AI interaction in a changing work environment. Practical implications: It is essential for organisations to focus on the transparency of AI, offer thorough training and ensure that tasks and technology align well to maximise the benefits of employee engagement from the implementation of AI. Originality/value: It offers a first comprehensive framework that integrates the Technology Acceptance Model, Job Demands-Resources theory and Human-AI Interaction to gain insights into the impact of AI on employee engagement.
